title: JavaScript OOP versus C# and TypeScript
hook: TypeScript classes look like C# in a slide deck, but the JavaScript runtime only has objects, prototype links, and functions. Interviews fail when you describe JavaScript OOP as nominal classes with virtual tables — the engine does prototype lookup and TypeScript erases types.

blocks.text: This topic compares **object-oriented programming (OOP)** from the JavaScript runtime perspective versus C# and TypeScript. C# types are **nominal** — the Common Language Runtime (CLR) loads type names, access modifiers, interface implementations, and virtual slots from Intermediate Language (IL) metadata. JavaScript has **objects and prototype chains** at runtime. TypeScript adds **structural** compile-time checks that **erase** when emitting JavaScript — interfaces and `private` keywords do not exist in the bundle.

entries.plainDefinition: Types match only when a declared relationship exists — same class or implements interface. C# uses nominal typing.
entries.example: Two classes with identical shapes but different names are not interchangeable in C#.

entries.plainDefinition: Types compatible when shapes match, regardless of name. TypeScript uses this at compile time.
entries.example: `const hint: AuthHint = { key: 's' }; const entry: CacheEntry = hint;` — allowed in TS.

entries.plainDefinition: Removing type information during compilation. TypeScript erases; C# preserves types in IL.
entries.example: A TypeScript interface does not exist in the emitted .js file.

entries.plainDefinition: Method lookup by walking the prototype chain. JavaScript alternative to CLR virtual method tables.
entries.example: `handler.parse(raw)` finds parse on instance or Constructor.prototype.

blocks.text: If you ship a .NET API and a TypeScript client, you debug them differently. On the server, `private` is enforced by CLR metadata — ordinary IL cannot read another type's private field. On the client, the bundle is plain objects: TypeScript `private` is gone, and only JavaScript `#fields` give runtime hiding. Auth tokens validated on the server are records with generated equality; the browser holds the same JSON as a plain object with `===` reference semantics and no `GetHashCode` contract.

blocks.title: The one-sentence summary
blocks.body: The TypeScript compiler strips types. The CLR loads them. JavaScript runs whatever is left — objects, prototypes, and functions.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

blocks.title: Tracing behavior from source to runtime

items.title: JavaScript: objects at runtime
items.body: Source compiles (or runs directly) to objects with [[Prototype]] links. Methods are properties found by prototype lookup.

items.title: TypeScript: compile-time only types
items.body: tsc removes interfaces, type aliases, and access modifiers. Output is JavaScript — class becomes constructor + prototype.

items.title: C#: IL plus CLR metadata
items.body: Roslyn emits IL with type names, virtual slots, and access modifiers. JIT compiles with that metadata intact.

items.title: Runtime type checks differ
items.body: C#: `if (handler is LtiHandler lti)`. JS/TS: `instanceof` works for class constructors only — not for erased TS interfaces.

snippet.label: Structural typing — allowed in TS, rejected in C#
snippet.explanation: Line 1–2: identical shapes, different names. Line 5: structural assign at compile time. Line 8–10: runtime is one plain object — no nominal type boundary.

snippet.label: Nominal typing enforced by the CLR
snippet.explanation: Line 1–2: same shape, different CLR types. Line 5: assignment rejected without declared relationship. Line 6: must copy explicitly — nominal boundary protects APIs.

snippet.label: Polymorphism — prototype lookup versus virtual dispatch
snippet.explanation: Line 11–12: lookup uses LtiHandler.prototype.parse. Line 14–15: mutating parent prototype affects instances without own override — no fixed vtable like C# virtual/override.

snippet.label: Privacy — # versus TS private versus C# private
snippet.explanation: Line 3: # enforced by engine. Line 8: cannot access outside class. Line 11–12: three-way privacy comparison — core interview fact.

blocks.title: Calling TypeScript private the same as C# private
blocks.body: TypeScript `private` is a compile-time check — the emitted JavaScript has no access restriction. C# `private` is enforced by CLR metadata. JavaScript `#field` is runtime-enforced but only within the class lexical scope.

blocks.title: Assuming instanceof checks TypeScript interfaces
blocks.body: `if (service instanceof IAttemptStore)` throws ReferenceError — interfaces erase. Use `instanceof` on classes or duck-type with no compiler guarantee.

blocks.text: The fundamental split from the JavaScript side: **everything is an object graph** with optional **class sugar** and optional **TypeScript annotations** that vanish. There is no CLR-style **metadata preservation** — stack traces show function names, not interface names. **Map** keys use SameValueZero (like `===` with NaN handling), not `GetHashCode`. **Records** in C# generate value equality; JavaScript spread `{ ...obj, key: v }` approximates `with` but shares nested references. **Production proof**: a .NET exception mentions `IAttemptStore.SaveAsync`; a Node.js trace shows `saveAsync` on a plain class prototype — never `IAttemptStore`. Cross-language API design: enforce nominal boundaries on the server; accept that the client bundle is structurally typed at best.

snippet.label: Runtime — no TypeScript interface equivalent
snippet.explanation: Line 9: instanceof checks prototype chain against class constructor. Line 14: interface names are not runtime values in JS/TS. Line 17: duck typing works but lacks C#-style contract enforcement.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying TypeScript and JavaScript OOP match C# because all three have classes — CLR keeps types; TS erases them; JS uses prototypes. Claiming TS private is runtime-enforced — inspect the bundle. Saying JavaScript has virtual dispatch like C# — prototype slots are mutable. Strong answer: runtime is objects + prototype chain; TS adds erased structural checks; C# adds nominal CLR metadata.

interviewTakeaways: JavaScript runtime: objects, prototype chain, functions — no CLR metadata or nominal types.
TypeScript types erase; interfaces and private keywords do not exist in the bundle unless emitted as # or runtime checks.
C# is nominally typed with virtual dispatch and real value types; JS uses prototype lookup and reference equality.

60s: JS runs objects and prototypes. TS adds compile-time structural types that erase. C# keeps CLR metadata — private, interfaces, virtual slots. instanceof works for JS classes, not TS interfaces. Privacy: # runtime, TS private erased, C# CLR enforced. Nominal vs structural is the API boundary difference.
Follow-up: give an assignment TypeScript allows that C# rejects at compile time.
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'TS classes equal C# classes at runtime.' Strong: TS erases to JS constructor + prototype — no CLR type identity.
Using instanceof on TypeScript interface names — ReferenceError after erasure.
Treating prototype lookup as C# virtual dispatch — JS prototypes can be mutated at runtime.

jsTsCorrelations.note: The TypeScript compiler strips types. The CLR loads them. JavaScript runs the erased output.
C# keeps interfaces and access modifiers at runtime; JavaScript has duck typing and # fields only.
